QUESTION OF THE WEEK - Ahead of Tuesday's RBA Board meeting, economists were surveyed on the outlook for interest rates. Briefly, a cut in March is seen as highly unlikely and the easing cycle may well be over. Economists see the next most likely move in rates as being a tightening later this year or early next year. However, renewed weakness in economic data and/or a better than expected outcome in the union movement's "living wage" case may change this outlook, economists said.

RETAIL TRADE - One of the most important figures of the week. After the weakness in December, and anecdotal evidence of improved trading in January, a solid rise is expected to reinforce perceptions of stronger economy in 1997. Economists said the data may not be as strong as some expect, because it may have been driven by discounting, keeping the nominal value of sales down.

BUILDING APPROVALS - Two months of declines, further reduction in interest rates and an improving housing sector all suggest a rise is due in this series. Economists expect that when abstracting from the monthly volatility of the data, approvals should show upward momentum through 1997.

QUARTERLY BALANCE OF PAYMENTS - Net exports should make a detraction from GDP growth as exports were disappointing in the quarter and imports rose in each month, and economists expect this to be reflected in the volumes data. Economsits said that as they had the monthly data, there should not be too much surprising in the quarterly figure, and GDP forecasts should not be altered too much following it.

GDP - Forecasts are stronger than they were at the beginning of the month, and may change again after the stocks data, but generally the GDP data is expected to confirm the moderate level of activity in the economy in mid to late 1996. While important, the perception that the easing cycle is over means that these figures will likely have little market impact, especially if they come in on expectations.

FOREIGN DEBT - With the exchange rate ending December basically steady with its end September level, the exchange rate should have little impact. A slight increase would reflect the ongoing current account deficit. Tuesday's quarterly balance of payments data will provide details of debt and equity financing of the deficit, and so help fine tune forecasts.
